stem: A 55-year-old man comes to the office due to progressive difficulty walking and frequent falls over the past year. Initially the patient had difficulty with balance when walking up and down the stairs. Now he has to brace himself against a wall even when walking on flat surfaces. He has had no urinary incontinence, slurred speech, or headaches. The patient was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension several years ago but is not compliant with medications. He also has a history of long-term, heavy alcohol and tobacco use. Blood pressure is 170/96 mm Hg and pulse is 84/min. The patient is alert and oriented. Bilateral pupils are equal and reactive. Extraocular movements are normal. Muscle bulk, tone, and strength are normal. Proprioception and vibration sensation are normal in the lower extremities. The patient exhibits a wide-based gait and is unable to perform tandem walking. Heel-knee-shin testing is abnormal but finger-nose testing is normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his ambulatory dysfunction?

options.A: Cerebellar degeneration due to alcohol neurotoxicity
options.B: Increased cerebrospinal fluid accumulation due to impaired absorption
options.C: Osteophytes causing progressive spinal cord compression
options.D: Peripheral nerve ischemia due to small vessel injury
options.F: Vascular disease causing multiple minor infarcts

explanations.B: Normal pressure hydrocephalus causes impaired CSF absorption resulting in the triad of gait disturbance, dementia, and urinary incontinence; this patient has intact cognition and no urinary symptoms.
explanations.C: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy causes upper motor neuron signs below the lesion and loss of vibration/proprioception, both absent here.
explanations.D: Diabetic distal symmetric polyneuropathy impairs distal sensation (vibration, light touch, pain), which is normal in this patient.
explanations.E: Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency presents with acute confusion, horizontal nystagmus/ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia, unlike this chronic, isolated cerebellar vermis atrophy.
explanations.F: Vascular dementia causes a stepwise cognitive decline and shuffling gait.
explanations.G: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration with loss of vibration/proprioception and spasticity.

generalExplanation:
This patient's progressive wide-based gait ataxia, impaired tandem walk, and abnormal heel-knee-shin testing with preserved upper extremity coordination (normal finger-nose testing) in the setting of chronic heavy alcohol use is classic for alcoholic cerebellar degeneration.

Alcohol neurotoxicity causes selective loss and atrophy of Purkinje cells in the anterior superior cerebellar vermis. Because the vermis coordinates truncal stability and lower-extremity postural control, patients develop truncal and gait ataxia, wide-based stance, and a pendular knee reflex, while the cerebellar hemispheres (controlling upper-limb fine motor skills) are relatively spared. Cessation of alcohol prevents disease progression, but ambulatory assistance devices are typically required.
educationalObjective: Alcoholic cerebellar degeneration results from selective Purkinje cell loss in the cerebellar vermis. It presents with slowly progressive wide-based gait ataxia and lower extremity postural incoordination with relative preservation of upper extremity fine coordination.

stem: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after having a seizure at school. His teacher says he suddenly fell to the ground with sustained flexion of the arms and extension of the legs, followed by clonic movements of his whole body for 5 minutes. The patient appeared sleepy after the episode, but his behavior is now at baseline. His parents arrive shortly after and note that the boy has been increasingly tired and irritable over the last few months, and his school performance has declined this semester. The patient has no medical issues and takes no medications. Physical examination shows decreased muscle strength on the left side of the body, with brisk deep-tendon reflexes in the left arm and leg. Visual field examination is normal. MRI of the brain reveals a space-occupying lesion in the right parietal lobe. Which of the following is most likely responsible for this patient's symptoms?

explanations.A: Craniopharyngiomas are sellar/suprasellar cystic calcified tumors causing bitemporal hemianopsia and hypopituitarism.
explanations.B: Ependymomas most commonly arise within the fourth ventricle in the posterior fossa in children, causing hydrocephalus and vomiting.
explanations.C: Glioblastoma is a high-grade, aggressive astrocytoma that presents hyperacutely over days to weeks rather than with insidious indolent progression over several months.
explanations.D: Medulloblastomas originate in the cerebellar vermis, presenting with truncal ataxia, morning headaches, and increased intracranial pressure.
explanations.F: Neuroblastomas originate from peripheral sympathetic chain tissues (adrenal medulla) and rarely present as primary intracerebral neoplasms.

generalExplanation:
Central nervous system tumors are the most common solid neoplasms in children. Astrocytomas (specifically low-grade pilocytic or diffuse astrocytomas) are the single most common pediatric brain tumors.

Supratentorial (cerebral hemispheric) tumors, such as this patient's right parietal mass, typically present with new-onset focal seizures (which may secondarily generalize), progressive personality or behavioral changes, declining academic performance, and focal contralateral neurological deficits (left hemiparesis and hyperreflexia). Because low-grade astrocytomas are slow-growing, symptoms develop indolently over several months. Brain MRI establishes tumor location and guides neurosurgical resection.
educationalObjective: Low-grade astrocytoma (pilocytic astrocytoma) is the most common pediatric brain tumor. When located in the supratentorial cerebral cortex, it frequently presents with new-onset seizures, headache, and contralateral focal motor deficits.

stem: A 2-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after a seizure. His mother says that he rolled off the bed last night while his older sister was changing his clothes and that he cried for a few minutes but fed well last night. Today, the patient had a tonic-clonic seizure that lasted 4 minutes after his morning feeding. He has been otherwise healthy. The patient was born at 31 weeks gestation, and his postnatal course was complicated by respiratory distress and hypoxia requiring intubation for several days. Height and weight are at the 50th percentile; head circumference is at the 98th percentile. Temperature is 36.7 C (98 F), blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg, and pulse is 144/min. Physical examination shows a limp infant who withdraws from painful stimuli. The anterior fontanelle is full and tense. Funduscopy reveals bilateral papilledema and retinal hemorrhages. The abdomen is soft with no hepatosplenomegaly. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of this patient's seizure?

explanations.A: Intraventricular hemorrhage with hydrocephalus can cause macrocephaly and seizures, but it manifests in the first days of life and does not produce retinal hemorrhages.
explanations.B: Metabolic derangements (hypocalcemia, hyponatremia) cause seizures but do not cause multilayered retinal hemorrhages or a bulging fontanelle.
explanations.C: Perinatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy presents with neonatal encephalopathy in the first 24-48 hours after birth, not after weeks of normal development.
explanations.D: Meningitis causes lethargy and bulging fontanelle accompanied by fever, and does not cause extensive retinal hemorrhages.
explanations.F: Arterial thromboembolism causes focal hemispheric infarcts without multilayered retinal hemorrhages.

generalExplanation:
This infant's presentation of new-onset seizures, a rapidly expanding head circumference, tense anterior fontanelle, and bilateral multilayered retinal hemorrhages is pathognomonic for abusive head trauma (shaken baby syndrome). Furthermore, the reported mechanism (rolling off a bed) is inconsistent with developmental capabilities, as rolling is normally acquired between 4 and 6 months.

Infants have heavy heads, weak neck muscles, and high brain water content. Violent repetitive shaking exerts massive acceleration-deceleration forces that tear and shear the fragile bridging veins traversing the subdural space, leading to subdural hematoma. Rapid vitreoretinal traction similarly shears retinal vessels, resulting in retinal hemorrhages. Urgent noncontrast head CT and a full skeletal survey are required, and child protective services must be notified immediately.
educationalObjective: Abusive head trauma (shaken baby syndrome) is characterized by subdural hematoma resulting from shearing of bridging veins, accompanied by bilateral retinal hemorrhages and injuries inconsistent with developmental stage.

stem: A 65-year-old man is being evaluated for new-onset ptosis. Earlier in the day, the patient underwent right total knee arthroplasty for advanced osteoarthritis with no operative complications. While in the postoperative recovery unit, he had difficulty opening his left eye and developed slurred speech. The patient has never had these symptoms, and his preoperative neurologic examination was unremarkable. He has no prior history of double vision, difficulty swallowing, or limb weakness. Medical history includes ischemic stroke with no residual deficits, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and a 20-pack-year smoking history. Temperature is 36.7 C (98.1 F), blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg, pulse is 92/min, and respirations are 12/min. Neurologic examination reveals bilateral ptosis, left greater than right. Pupils are equal in size and reactive to light. An ice pack is placed over the closed eyelids for 2 minutes, leading to improvement of the ptosis. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current symptoms?

options.D: Inflammation and edema of the facial nerve

explanations.B: Horner syndrome produces ptosis and miosis due to sympathetic disruption; the ice pack test is negative.
explanations.C: Lambert-Eaton syndrome involves presynaptic P/Q-type calcium channel antibodies, primarily causing proximal lower extremity weakness with hyporeflexia that improves following exertion.
explanations.D: Bell palsy involves CN VII, producing lower motor neuron facial paralysis with inability to close the eye (lagophthalmos), rather than ptosis.
explanations.E: Diabetic CN III neuropathy causes 'down-and-out' ophthalmoplegia with pupil sparing, which does not improve with cooling.
explanations.F: Compressive CN III palsy from a PCoA aneurysm causes a fixed, dilated pupil and ophthalmoplegia.

generalExplanation:
This patient's new-onset fluctuating ptosis and dysarthria following general anesthesia (where exposure to nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents like rocuronium unmasks subclinical disease) and prompt improvement with the bedside ice pack test point to myasthenia gravis (MG).

MG is mediated by autoantibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChR) at the neuromuscular junction. Cold temperatures inhibit acetylcholinesterase activity, retarding the breakdown of acetylcholine and transiently increasing acetylcholine concentration in the synaptic cleft. A positive ice pack test (>=2 mm improvement in palpebral fissure width after 2 minutes) is highly specific for MG. Confirmatory testing is performed with serum AChR binding antibodies, followed by chest CT to evaluate for thymoma.
educationalObjective: Myasthenia gravis is caused by autoantibodies directed against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors. The bedside ice pack test supports the diagnosis when cold application improves ptosis by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase and increasing acetylcholine availability.

stem: A 48-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to 3 days of nausea and vomiting. For the past 4 weeks, the patient has also had increasingly severe headaches. He had a kidney transplant 2 years ago for glomerulonephritis and takes immunosuppressants. Temperature is 38.2 C (100.7 F), blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg, and pulse is 70/min. The patient is awake but drowsy. Examination shows neck stiffness. Cranial nerves are intact. Muscle strength is normal, but deep tendon reflexes are brisk. CT scan of the head shows no other abnormalities. Results of cerebrospinal fluid analysis show glucose 25 mg/dL, protein 110 mg/dL, white blood cells 70/mm3 (95% lymphocytes), and red blood cells 1/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

explanations.B: Herpes simplex encephalitis presents acutely with fever, temporal lobe seizures, altered mentation, and CSF with prominent erythrocytes and normal glucose.
explanations.C: Pneumococcal meningitis is an acute, fulminant infection presenting within hours/days with marked neutrophilic pleocytosis (>1,000 WBCs) and very high protein.
explanations.D: Subarachnoid hemorrhage presents with sudden thunderclap headache, and CSF shows elevated RBCs without clearance across collection tubes and xanthochromia.
explanations.E: Cerebral toxoplasmosis presents with multiple ring-enhancing parenchymal lesions on brain imaging in patients with advanced AIDS (CD4 <100/mm3).

generalExplanation:
In an immunosuppressed patient (renal transplant recipient on maintenance immunosuppression), subacute meningitis presenting over weeks with indolent headache, vomiting, low-grade fever, and nuchal rigidity is characteristic of Cryptococcus neoformans infection.

Cryptococcal capsular polysaccharides clog arachnoid villi, producing elevated opening pressure and symptoms of intracranial hypertension. Classic CSF findings include:
• Mild to moderate lymphocytic pleocytosis (typically <100-500 WBCs/mm3)
• Moderately elevated protein (100-200 mg/dL)
• Markedly decreased glucose (<40 mg/dL or CSF:serum ratio <0.4)
Diagnosis is confirmed by CSF cryptococcal antigen testing (CrAg, sensitivity/specificity >95%) or India ink capsule staining. Initial treatment is induction therapy with intravenous amphotericin B plus flucytosine, followed by long-term oral fluconazole.
educationalObjective: Cryptococcal meningitis occurs in immunocompromised individuals (solid organ transplant, HIV) and presents subacutely with headache, fever, and meningismus. CSF analysis reveals lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose, and elevated protein; confirmation is by cryptococcal antigen testing.

stem: A 9-month-old girl is brought to the clinic for left eye redness and tearing that began last evening. Temperature is 37 C (98.6 F), pulse is 130/min, and respirations are 30/min. Examination of the left eye shows clear tearing on the eyelashes with conjunctival erythema. The left cornea and globe are larger than the right. The patient blinks frequently and turns away when light is shined in the left eye. Extraocular muscle movements are intact and appear nonpainful. The patient has a port-wine stain overlying the left forehead, eyelids, and cheek. Her mother says the lesion is more erythematous than normal, but there is no tenderness, warmth, or pruritus on examination. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?

explanations.A: Topical antibiotics treat bacterial conjunctivitis, which causes purulent discharge and matting of eyelids without globe or corneal enlargement.
explanations.B: Eye drainage cultures evaluate neonatal purulent ophthalmia (gonococcus/chlamydia), not buphthalmos and port-wine stain.
explanations.C: Nasolacrimal duct massage treats congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction, which presents with chronic tearing without photophobia, corneal edema, or buphthalmos.
explanations.D: Oral antibiotics treat preseptal cellulitis, characterized by eyelid erythema and warmth without corneal enlargement.
explanations.F: Antihistamine drops treat allergic conjunctivitis, which causes bilateral pruritus without buphthalmos.

generalExplanation:
This infant presents with buphthalmos (enlarged globe and cornea), epiphora (excessive tearing), photophobia, and blepharospasm in the eye ipsilateral to a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus in the V1/V2 trigeminal distribution), which is diagnostic of glaucoma associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS).

SWS is a congenital neurocutaneous disorder caused by somatic mosaic mutations in the GNAQ gene, characterized by facial angiomas, ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis, and secondary glaucoma (due to anterior chamber angle dysgenesis and elevated episcleral venous pressure). Elevated intraocular pressure in infancy causes mechanical stretching and enlargement of the pliable infant sclera and cornea. Urgent tonometry to measure intraocular pressure is required, followed by surgical intervention (goniotomy or trabeculotomy) to preserve visual acuity.
educationalObjective: Infantile glaucoma presents with epiphora, photophobia, blepharospasm, and an enlarged globe/cornea (buphthalmos). It is strongly associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome in infants with an ipsilateral facial port-wine stain. Diagnosis requires tonometry.

stem: A 65-year-old woman comes to the office for evaluation of progressively worsening memory. The patient lives alone and considers herself "very independent"; however, she has recently forgotten to pay her bills on several occasions and also lost her way while driving in a previously familiar neighborhood 2 weeks ago. Review of systems reveals no other symptoms except for mild urinary urgency. The patient has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. She does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Temperature is 36.7 C (98 F), blood pressure is 130/90 mm Hg, pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 14/min. The lungs are clear to auscultation, and a grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur is present. Abdominal examination shows no tenderness or masses. The cranial nerves are intact, funduscopy is normal, and there is no tremor. The patient immediately recalls all 3 of 3 items read to her, but 5 minutes later she can remember none of them. Her gait is broad-based and shuffling. Blood cell count and serum chemistry studies are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?

options.D: Neurocognitive effects of vitamin B12 deficiency

explanations.A: Alpha-synuclein accumulation in the substantia nigra occurs in Parkinson disease, characterized by resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, and late dementia.
explanations.C: Beta-amyloid neuritic plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles characterize Alzheimer disease; memory loss is isolated early, and gait impairment/incontinence occur only in late-stage disease.
explanations.D: B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration with loss of vibration/proprioception and megaloblastic anemia.
explanations.E: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration causes early personality alteration, disinhibition, or primary progressive aphasia.

generalExplanation:
This patient presents with the classic triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH):
1. Gait disturbance: A slow, broad-based, shuffling 'magnetic' gait (appearing glued to the floor)
2. Cognitive impairment: Psychomotor slowing, executive dysfunction, and memory decline
3. Urinary symptoms: Early urinary urgency progressing to overt incontinence

NPH is caused by impaired cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) absorption at the arachnoid granulations. The resulting accumulation of CSF leads to ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cerebral sulcal atrophy. Mechanical stretching of the sacral motor fibers in the corona radiata and periventricular white matter tracts accounts for the classic triad. The diagnosis is confirmed by transient symptomatic gait improvement following a high-volume lumbar puncture (Miller Fisher tap test), and definitive treatment is surgical ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement.
educationalObjective: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is caused by decreased cerebrospinal fluid absorption at the arachnoid villi, resulting in ventriculomegaly. It is characterized by the clinical triad of gait disturbance ('magnetic' gait), cognitive impairment, and urinary urgency/incontinence.

stem: A 40-year-old man comes to the office due to coughing while drinking. Over the past 2 months, the patient has been coughing when he drinks water because it "goes down the wrong pipe." On occasion, water will come out of his nose when drinking. Also, his speech sounds slurred and nasal. The patient has no medical conditions and takes no medications. On examination, there are no mucosal lesions in the oral cavity or oropharynx. Palate elevation is sluggish on the right side. The tongue appears thin and there are fasciculations. When the physician taps on the chin while the mouth is slightly open, the jaw jerks forward briskly. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish a diagnosis in this patient?

explanations.A: AChR antibodies evaluate myasthenia gravis, which causes fatigable bulbar weakness without pathologic hyperreflexia (brisk jaw jerk) or tongue fasciculations.
explanations.B: Cervical spine imaging evaluates cervical cord compression, but bulbar motor cranial nerve nuclei and the jaw jerk reflex are located above the foramen magnum.
explanations.D: Muscle biopsy evaluates inflammatory myopathies (polymyositis), which do not produce upper motor neuron signs.
explanations.E: Serum CK evaluates primary muscular dystrophies or rhabdomyolysis, which lack upper motor neuron signs.
explanations.F: Serum botulinum toxin assay evaluates botulism, which produces acute descending paralysis without hyperreflexia.

generalExplanation:
This patient has bulbar-onset amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), demonstrating the coexistence of upper motor neuron (UMN) and lower motor neuron (LMN) lesions localized to bulbar cranial nerve territories:
• LMN signs: Tongue atrophy and visible fasciculations (denervation of the hypoglossal nucleus [CN XII])
• UMN signs: Pathologic hyperactive jaw jerk reflex (loss of bilateral corticobulbar inhibitory control over the trigeminal motor nucleus [CN V])
• Bulbar dysfunction: Palatal weakness causing liquid regurgitation through the nose and hypernasal dysarthria

Electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction studies are the gold standard diagnostic tests to establish ALS by demonstrating widespread acute and chronic denervation (fibrillations, positive sharp waves, and fasciculation potentials) across multiple body segments (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral). Brain and spinal MRI are obtained to rule out structural mimics.
educationalObjective: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with bulbar onset presents with dysarthria, dysphagia, and nasal regurgitation, combining upper motor neuron signs (pathologic brisk jaw jerk) and lower motor neuron signs (tongue atrophy and fasciculations). Electromyography is the definitive test to demonstrate widespread denervation.

stem: A 70-year-old man comes to the office 4 weeks after experiencing an ischemic stroke. Medical history is significant for long standing hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Vital signs are unremarkable. BMI is 24 kg/m2. The patient is right-handed. Only the right side of his face is shaved. When asked to raise his left arm, the patient raises his right. When asked to fill in the numbers of a clock, he puts numbers only on the right side. Which of the following areas is most likely affected by the stroke in this patient?

explanations.A: Left frontal lesions cause Broca expressive aphasia and contralateral right hemiparesis.
explanations.B: Left temporal lesions cause Wernicke receptive aphasia with fluent word salad and lack of comprehension.
explanations.C: Right frontal lesions cause left hemiparesis, conjugate gaze deviation to the right, and executive dysfunction.
explanations.D: Right occipital lesions cause left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, but patients recognize that they cannot see the left visual field (no hemineglect).

generalExplanation:
This patient exhibits classic hemispatial neglect syndrome (hemineglect), manifested by ignoring sensory and spatial stimuli on the left side of his body and environment (shaving only the right side of his face, drawing clock numbers only on the right half, and failing to acknowledge his left arm).

Hemispatial neglect is characteristically caused by an ischemic stroke involving the nondominant (usually right) parietal cortex. The right parietal cortex is uniquely responsible for spatial attention and orientation across both the right and left visual fields, whereas the left parietal cortex attends primarily to the right side. Consequently, damage to the right parietal lobe leaves the left hemispace unattended.
educationalObjective: Hemispatial neglect syndrome (ignoring sensory/visual stimuli on the contralateral side, eg, drawing only half of a clock) is caused by a lesion in the nondominant (typically right) parietal cortex, which mediates spatial attention.

stem: A 36-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to severe headache and vision disturbance. The symptoms began abruptly an hour ago, and since then she has also felt weak, dizzy, and nauseated. The patient has had no similar symptoms in the past. Medical history is significant for a prolactinoma diagnosed a month ago, which is being treated with cabergoline. She does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Temperature is 37.6 C (99.7 F), supine blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg with a decrease to 60/40 mm Hg on standing, and pulse is 110/min. On physical examination, the patient appears anxious and in moderate distress. There is mild ptosis and impaired adduction on the right. Bitemporal hemianopsia is present. Bilateral upper and lower extremity muscle strength and sensation are normal. The neck veins are flat, heart and lung sounds are normal, and there is no abdominal tenderness or extremity edema. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's hemodynamic changes?

explanations.B: Dopamine agonists (cabergoline) can cause mild orthostatic dizziness, but do not produce sudden apoplectic headache, bitemporal hemianopsia, CN III palsy, and distributive shock.
explanations.C: Elevated ICP causes Cushing triad (hypertension and bradycardia), the exact opposite of this patient's severe hypotension and tachycardia.
explanations.D: Neurogenic shock occurs with high cervical/thoracic spinal cord transection and presents with hypotension accompanied by bradycardia, not reflex tachycardia.
explanations.E: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage does not cause acute panhypopituitarism and acute adrenal crisis with distributive shock.

generalExplanation:
This patient has pituitary apoplexy, an acute, life-threatening neurological and endocrine emergency caused by sudden infarction or hemorrhage into a preexisting pituitary adenoma (eg, prolactinoma). Rapid expansion within the rigid bony sella turcica leads to severe thunderclap headache, optic chiasm compression (bitemporal hemianopsia), and cavernous sinus compression (right CN III palsy with ptosis and impaired adduction).

Critically, acute pituitary gland destruction precipitates acute secondary adrenal insufficiency (adrenal crisis) due to the abrupt cessation of ACTH release. Without cortisol, vascular responsiveness to catecholamines is lost, resulting in profound vasodilation, refractory hypotension, and distributive circulatory shock. Immediate management requires aggressive isotonic volume resuscitation and stress-dose intravenous glucocorticoids (hydrocortisone or dexamethasone), followed by emergent neurosurgical decompression.
educationalObjective: Pituitary apoplexy causes sudden severe headache, visual field cuts (bitemporal hemianopsia), and ophthalmoplegia due to bleeding into a pituitary adenoma. The immediate life threat is acute adrenal crisis from loss of ACTH-cortisol support, causing refractory hypotension and shock.
